title: Infra that fixes itself, thanks to coding agents — Mahmoud Abdelwahab, Railway
talk_summary: Mahmoud Abdelwahab demos a self-healing infra loop on Railway: a scheduled durable workflow pulls project architecture, resource and HTTP metrics, filters services exceeding thresholds over a time slice, enriches with logs and context, has an LLM write a fix plan, then hands it to a headless OpenCode server that clones the repo and opens a PR for human review. The core transferable ideas are durable execution with cached steps, time-slice threshold analysis instead of noisy alerts, and a headless coding-agent server as a service.

takeaways.technique: Durable workflow with per-step caching and retries
takeaways.what_they_do: Each workflow step's result is cached on success and steps auto-retry, so a failed run resumes where it left off instead of redoing API calls and LLM work.
takeaways.evidence_quote: each step when it succeeds uh the result is cached ... we won't really repeat any work, which is one awesome because it's faster, but also it's more cost effective

takeaways.what_they_do: A cron workflow every 10-30 min fetches architecture, CPU/memory and HTTP error/latency metrics, flags services over thresholds, and emits a list of affected services that feed a fix-generation workflow.
takeaways.evidence_quote: a workflow that runs on a schedule ... fetch each services resource metrics ... which services have exceeded which thresholds ... return a list of the affected services

takeaways.technique: Time-slice analysis instead of threshold alerts
takeaways.what_they_do: Rather than firing on a single threshold breach, they analyze a window of metrics plus logs to avoid noisy false positives from spiky workloads.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it's probably better to be able to analyze a slice of time rather than just having a threshold being met because it can get pretty noisy

takeaways.what_they_do: After flagging a service they pull additional context (HTTP/build/deploy logs, architecture summary as markdown) and only then ask an LLM to write a detailed fix plan, which is passed to the coding agent.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we can just write a detail plan ... we just then give this plan to an agent and then the agent will just follow the process

takeaways.technique: Headless coding-agent server as a deployable service
takeaways.what_they_do: They run OpenCode as a headless server (createOpenCodeServer) in a Docker image with git, gh CLI, curl, jq preinstalled, and drive it via API; each repo gets its own session.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can have a a a headless server that runs that exposes an API for you to essentially interact with an agent

takeaways.technique: Agent-authored PR with structured root-cause summary
takeaways.what_they_do: The coding agent opens a PR whose description includes analysis summary, root causes, and what was fixed, so a human only reviews the PR instead of investigating.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we have a summary of all the changes, uh, an analysis summary, the root causes, what was fixed
